segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In those days, when there was again a large crowd and they had nothing to eat, he called the disciples to him and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I feel compassion for the crowd, because they have stayed with me three days now and have nothing to eat.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If I send them away hungry to their homes, they will collapse on the way—and some of them have come from far away.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where could anyone get enough bread to satisfy these people here in a deserted place?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He asked them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How many loaves do you have?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Seven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He directed the crowd to sit down on the ground. Then he took the seven loaves, gave thanks, broke them, and gave them to his disciples to set before the people, and they set them before the crowd.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They also had a few small fish; and after blessing them, he said that these too were to be set before them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They ate and were satisfied, and they picked up the leftover pieces—seven large baskets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There were about four thousand people. And he sent them away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees came out and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven, to test him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Sighing deeply in his spirit, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And leaving them, he got into the boat again and went away to the other side.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now they had forgotten to bring bread, and except for one loaf they had none with them in the boat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he warned them, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Watch out! Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were discussing with one another the fact that they had no bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Aware of this, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of pieces you picked up?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Twelve.”

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And when I broke the seven for the four thousand, how many large baskets full of pieces did you pick up?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Seven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you not yet understand?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to Bethsaida. And some people brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village; and after spitting on his eyes and laying his hands on him, he asked him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you see anything?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He looked up and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I see people; I see them like trees, walking around.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he laid his hands on his eyes again; and the man looked intently, and his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he sent him home, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not even go into the village.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus and his disciples went out to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who do people say that I am?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They told him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “John the Baptist; and others say Elijah; and still others, one of the prophets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he asked them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “But you—who do you say that I am?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are the Messiah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he sternly ordered them to tell no one about him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said this plainly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he turned and, seeing his disciples, rebuked Peter and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God but on the things of people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he called the crowd to him along with his disciples and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If anyone wants to come after me, let them deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake and for the sake of the good news will save it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For what does it profit a person to gain the whole world and forfeit their life?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For what could a person give in exchange for their life?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of that person when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”

notes.note: The Greek word here names a different kind of basket from the one used in the feeding of the five thousand, generally a larger hamper; the same word is used for the basket in which Paul was lowered from the wall of Damascus. Mark keeps the two words apart again in verses 19 and 20, so the translation distinguishes them as well.

The place is otherwise unknown. The parallel account in Matthew names “Magadan” instead, and some manuscripts of Mark substitute that name or “Magdala.” It was presumably on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, but its location is uncertain.
Older English versions have “tempting him.” The verb means to put someone to the test, here by a demand meant to discredit him, and most modern translations also use “test” in this verse.

notes.phrase: no sign will be given to this generation
notes.note: The Greek is literally “if a sign will be given to this generation,” a Hebrew-style oath formula in which the penalty clause is left unspoken. It amounts to an emphatic denial, and translations regularly render it as one.

Leaven was a piece of fermented dough kept back to raise the next batch, and it was a common image for a small influence that works through the whole, often a corrupting one. Many modern versions say “yeast”; “leaven” is kept as the more exact term. Mark does not say what the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod is, though the parallels in Matthew and Luke each give an explanation.

notes.phrase: “Do not even go into the village.”
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add “nor tell anyone in the village,” and others combine the two commands in different ways. The shorter reading translated here has the earliest support and is the one adopted in most modern editions.

The traditional rendering is “the Christ.” The Greek word translates the Hebrew title for the anointed king Israel expected, and Peter is using it as a title, not a name, which “Messiah” conveys to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it functions as a name.

The Greek word can mean speaking without figures or reserve, or speaking in public view. The King James Version has “openly”; most modern translations have “plainly,” which suits the contrast with Jesus’ earlier indirect teaching. On either reading the point is that he held nothing back.

The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which today sounds like a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

Many versions switch to “soul” in verses 36 and 37, while others keep “life.” The Greek word is the same one translated “life” in verse 35, and the argument depends on that continuity. In first-century usage it most often means a person’s life or living self and not an immaterial part of them, though the saying plainly has more in view than physical survival.

In the prophets, Israel’s unfaithfulness to God is regularly pictured as a wife’s adultery. The word carries that sense here: a generation unfaithful to God. It is not a comment on sexual conduct in particular.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Synoptics of Jesus and in parables; translators vary between “have compassion,” “be moved with pity,” and “feel sorry for,” and readers should see one rendering.

candidates.rendering: rebuke; sternly order (with a following command)
candidates.reason: The same verb covers rebuking people, demons, and wind and also sternly charging to silence; Mark repeats it in 8:30–33, and a fixed policy is needed on when to split the senses.
Very frequent in the Gospels and Acts; “scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers, while alternatives such as “teachers of the law” or “legal experts” are used by other versions.
Occurs in the Gospels and Paul as a fixed metaphor; versions split between “leaven” and “yeast,” and the image should read the same everywhere.
With ἔρημος and ἔρημος τόπος it is rendered variously as “wilderness,” “desert,” and “deserted place,” which obscures links between the feeding stories and the Exodus wilderness background.
